title: Notice, question, predict
target: Use observations to make a prediction that can be tested.
cpa_model: Evidence is what the data show. A prediction says what you expect next. Example: positions 2, 4, 6 m at one-second intervals suggest 8 m next, if the pattern continues.
honors_model: A defensible model states evidence, a prediction, an assumption, and a possible test. Our asteroid 2026-XJ is a fictional classroom case, not a real alert.

cpa.title: Read a scale
cpa.prompt: A ruler shows a toy car at 2 cm, then at 7 cm. Draw both positions and the change. How far apart are the marks?
cpa.answer: Marks 5 cm apart; rightward arrow from 2 to 7 cm.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw a position strip for these four times. Mark which point is a prediction rather than an observation.
cpa.answer: Four equally spaced points; the 11 m point is the prediction. A new measurement could disagree.
cpa.reference:
Δx = x_f - x_i; x_next = x_now + Δx.
For a repeating position pattern only. i = initial; f = final. Check the pattern against evidence.
cpa.worked: A cart is at 2, 5 and 8 m at 0, 1 and 2 s. Equal jumps of 3 m suggest 11 m at 3 s, if the pattern continues.

cpa.title: Notice a pattern
cpa.prompt: These are supplied cart observations, one second apart. Write two things you notice. Circle the part of the display that supports each notice.
cpa.answer: Positions increase by 2 m each second; the cart moves right with equal displacements in equal times. Accept observations tied to the displayed values.

cpa.title: Make a prediction
cpa.prompt: Use the cart observations in 3. Predict its position at 3 s. Show how you extended the pattern.
cpa.answer: 7 m: another +2 m from 5 m. Assumes the same velocity continues.

cpa.title: Evidence or a claim?
cpa.prompt: Fictional briefing: “An object is approaching Earth. Its future path is uncertain.” Mark each E (stated evidence) or C (claim not established): approaching Earth; guaranteed impact; uncertain path.
cpa.answer: E, C, E. Approaching alone does not establish impact.

cpa.title: Test the model
cpa.prompt: A different cart is observed at 9, 7, 5 m at 0, 1, 2 s. Predict its position at 3 s. What would a new reading of 4 m make you check?
cpa.answer: 3 m if the -2 m each second pattern continues. Check measurement quality and whether motion changed.

cpa.title: Ask a useful question
cpa.prompt: Change “Is the asteroid bad?” into a question you could investigate. Name one measurement you would need.
cpa.answer: Examples: Where will it be in a month? Need repeated positions, velocity direction and time. How large is it? Need observations of size. Accept a measurable question and matching evidence.
cpa.frame: I could investigate ____. I would measure ____.

cpa.title: Choose useful evidence
cpa.prompt: Two groups time the same toy car over the same marked track. One records three times; the other writes "pretty fast." Which record would let someone check the claim? Explain.
cpa.answer: The measured times with the track distance allow calculation and repetition. The phrase alone gives no measurable comparison.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: A cart is at 0, 3, 6 m at 0, 1, 2 s. Predict its position at 4 s. Include one assumption and one observation that could challenge your prediction.
cpa.answer: 12 m, assuming +3 m each second continues. A later position inconsistent with that prediction, beyond measurement variation, challenges the model.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Return to the worked example in problem 2. Create two possible positions at 4 s if the cart changes its motion after 2 s. Draw both possibilities. What measurement would help choose between them?
cpa.answer: Many answers: continuing gives 14 m; stopping at 2 s gives 8 m. Observe later positions and times.

honors.title: Read a scale
honors.prompt: A ruler shows a toy car at 2 cm, then at 7 cm. Draw both positions and the change. How far apart are the marks?
honors.answer: Marks 5 cm apart; rightward arrow from 2 to 7 cm.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Draw a position strip for these four times. Mark which point is a prediction rather than an observation.
honors.answer: Four equally spaced points; the 11 m point is the prediction. A new measurement could disagree.
honors.reference:
Δx = x_f - x_i; x_next = x_now + Δx.
For a repeating position pattern only. i = initial; f = final. Check the pattern against evidence.
honors.worked: A cart is at 2, 5 and 8 m at 0, 1 and 2 s. Equal jumps of 3 m suggest 11 m at 3 s, if the pattern continues.

honors.title: Extract the evidence
honors.prompt: Fictional briefing: “Repeated images show an object approaching Earth’s neighborhood. Its path and size remain uncertain.” Give two supported observations and one unsupported conclusion.
honors.answer: Approach and uncertainty are stated. Impact, a precise arrival date, or a damage estimate is not established.

honors.title: Fit a simple model
honors.prompt: Use the supplied cart data. State a rule for position as a function of time and predict x at 5 s. Explain why this is a model, not a guarantee.
honors.answer: x = 1 + 3 t in meters, with t in seconds; x(5)=16 m. Assumes constant velocity beyond the observed interval.

honors.title: Challenge the prediction
honors.prompt: For the cart in 4, a new measurement at 5 s is 14.0 ± 0.2 m. Is it consistent with your exact constant-velocity prediction? Give two possible explanations.
honors.answer: Prediction 16 m lies outside 13.8-14.2 m. Motion may have changed or earlier measurements/model assumptions may be wrong. Do not infer a specific cause without evidence.

honors.title: Design the observation
honors.prompt: You can request two new observations of the fictional asteroid. Specify what, when, and how each would improve a position prediction.
honors.answer: Positions in a stated frame at two known times estimate velocity including direction. Other justified observations accepted; must explain how they improve the prediction.

honors.title: Compare claims
honors.prompt: Claim A: “A straight-line model predicts where it may be.” Claim B: “The asteroid will hit Earth.” Explain what additional evidence and physics separate these claims.
honors.answer: Need positions of both bodies at the same time, gravitational/orbital changes, 3 D state and uncertainty. A simplified model alone cannot establish real impact.

honors.title: Choose useful evidence
honors.prompt: Two groups time the same toy car over the same marked track. One records three times; the other writes "pretty fast." Which record would let someone check the claim? Explain.
honors.answer: The measured times with the track distance allow calculation and repetition. The phrase alone gives no measurable comparison.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: Supplied positions are 12, 8, 4 m at 0, 2, 4 s. Predict x at 7 s. State the rate, your assumption, and a future observation that would test it.
honors.answer: v=-2 m/s; x=12-2(7)=-2 m. Assumes constant velocity. Measure x at a stated later time and compare with the model including uncertainty.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: Return to the worked example in problem 2. Construct two position rules that match all three observations in the worked case but disagree at 4 s. Explain why the data do not guarantee either extrapolation.
honors.answer: One rule x=2+3 t throughout; another follows that rule through 2 s then stays at 8 m. At 4 s: 14 m versus 8 m; future behavior is unmeasured.

criteria: Separate stated evidence from unsupported claims.
Extend a position pattern and state an assumption.
Name an observation that could test the prediction.

title: Position, distance, displacement
target: Distinguish a location, a total path length, and a change in position.
cpa_model: Distance counts every part of the path. Displacement joins start to finish. Example: start 0 m, go to 4 m, return to 1 m. Distance = 4 + 3 = 7 m; displacement = 1 m right.
honors_model: Choose an origin and positive direction first. Position: x. Displacement: Δx = x_final - x_initial. Total distance: sum the lengths of every leg. A coordinate sign does not tell the direction of motion.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A cart is at 3, 8, 13 m at 0, 1, 2 s. Predict its position at 7 s. State an assumption and a measurement that could challenge it.
cpa.answer: 38 m if the 5 m/s rightward motion continues. Check a later timed position against the prediction.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw the two route arrows and a separate start-to-finish arrow. Label the length of each.
cpa.answer: Route arrows 4 m right and 2 m left; resultant 2 m right.
cpa.reference:
Δx = x_f - x_i; distance = sum of path lengths.
Choose an origin and positive direction. i = initial; f = final.
cpa.worked: A walker starts at 2 m, reaches 6 m, then ends at 4 m. Distance=4+2=6 m. Displacement=4-2=2 m right.

cpa.title: Read the route
cpa.prompt: The route starts at 1 m, goes to 6 m, and ends at 3 m. Label start, turn, and end on the picture.
cpa.answer: Start 1 m, turn 6 m, end 3 m.

cpa.title: Count the whole path
cpa.prompt: For the route in 3, find each leg and the total distance. First leg: ____ m. Return leg: ____ m. Total: ____ m.

cpa.title: Connect start to finish
cpa.prompt: For the same route, draw one arrow from start to end. Give the displacement and final position. Are they the same number?
cpa.answer: Displacement 2 m right; final position 3 m. They differ because the start was 1 m, not zero.
cpa.frame: I end ____ m to the ____ of where I started.

cpa.title: A complete trip back
cpa.prompt: Start at 0 m. Walk 5 m east, then 5 m west. Find distance and displacement. Explain why one is zero.
cpa.answer: Distance 10 m; displacement 0 m because start and end coincide.

cpa.title: Fix the wording
cpa.prompt: A student says, “My displacement was 8 m because I walked 8 m altogether.” Must that be true? Use a short route or sketch to explain.
cpa.answer: No. Distance is path length. Example: 4 m out and 4 m back gives 8 m distance and zero displacement.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A cart is observed at 3, 8, 13 m, one second apart. Record two patterns and point to values that support each.
cpa.answer: Position increases by 5 m each second; equal rightward changes suggest steady motion.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: Start at 2 m, move to 7 m, and finish at 5 m. Find total distance, displacement with direction, and final position.
cpa.answer: Distance 5+2=7 m; displacement 3 m right; final position 5 m.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Design two routes that start at 1 m and end at 4 m: one of distance 3 m and one of distance 7 m. Draw and check both.
cpa.answer: Direct 1 to 4: 3 m. Route 1 to 6 to 4: 5+2=7 m. Both displacements 3 m right.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: Positions are 15, 10, 5 m at 0, 2, 4 s. Predict position at 7 s. Give the rate, an assumption and a future test.
honors.answer: v=-2.5 m/s; x(7)=-2.5 m. Assumes constant velocity; compare another timed position with its uncertainty.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Draw the two route arrows and a separate start-to-finish arrow. Label the length of each.
honors.answer: Route arrows 4 m right and 2 m left; resultant 2 m right.
honors.reference:
Δx = x_f - x_i; distance = sum of path lengths.
Choose an origin and positive direction. i = initial; f = final.
honors.worked: A walker starts at 2 m, reaches 6 m, then ends at 4 m. Distance=4+2=6 m. Displacement=4-2=2 m right.

honors.title: Track a signed route
honors.prompt: East is positive. Start at -3 m, go to +4 m, then end at -1 m. Sketch the route and calculate distance and displacement.
honors.answer: Distance 7+5=12 m; displacement -1-(-3)=+2 m.

honors.title: Change the coordinate convention
honors.prompt: For the route in 3, reverse the positive direction while keeping the origin fixed. Give the new endpoint coordinates and displacement. What stays unchanged?
honors.answer: Coordinates become +3,-4,+1 m; displacement -2 m. Physical route, distance 12 m, and displacement direction are unchanged.

honors.title: A closed path
honors.prompt: A runner completes one 400 m lap, then runs another 100 m around a circular track. Is the displacement magnitude 500 m? Explain what would be needed to calculate it.
honors.answer: No. Distance is 500 m. Need geometry/start/end positions; displacement is the chord from start to end, not the arc length. Full lap contributes zero displacement.

honors.title: Different paths, same endpoints
honors.prompt: Sketch two different routes from (0, 0) m to (4, 3) m. Give each path distance and the common displacement magnitude.
honors.answer: Examples: east then north gives 7 m; direct diagonal gives 5 m. Both displacement (4, 3) m, magnitude 5 m.

honors.title: Zero and nonzero
honors.prompt: Can displacement be zero while distance is nonzero? Can distance be zero while displacement is nonzero? Justify both answers.
honors.answer: Yes: return trip. No: nonzero displacement requires a path of nonzero length; distance is at least displacement magnitude.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: A fictional observing report records 3 images of a moving object but gives no distance or size calibration. State a supported observation and explain why a precise impact prediction is unsupported.
honors.answer: Motion is reported across 3 images. Uncalibrated images do not establish size, distance, full trajectory or impact; more measurements and uncertainties are needed.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: Start at +5 m, walk to -2 m, and finish at +1 m. Calculate distance and displacement. Explain why neither equals final position.
honors.answer: Distance 7+3=10 m; displacement 1-5=-4 m; final position +1 m. They describe path length, change, and location respectively.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: In one dimension, start at -2 m and end at +3 m with total distance 11 m. Find two possible single-turn positions and draw both routes.
honors.answer: Turn at +6 m: 8+3=11 m; or -5 m: 3+8=11 m. Displacement +5 m in either case.

criteria: Label the origin, start, turn and finish.
Calculate path distance and signed displacement separately.
Explain why position and displacement can differ.

title: Velocity and position graphs
target: Connect a position-time graph to velocity using slope.
cpa_model: Velocity tells how position changes each second. Example: from 1 m to 7 m in 3 s, change = 6 m, so velocity = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s right. A flat position graph means no position change.
honors_model: Average velocity = Δx/Δt. Average speed = total distance/total time. A straight position-time segment has constant velocity equal to its slope; graph height is position, not velocity.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: Start at 3 m, move to 10 m, then finish at 5 m. Draw the route. Find distance, displacement with direction and final position.
cpa.answer: Distance 12 m; displacement +2 m (right); final position 5 m.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Sketch the graph through the two points. Draw and label the rise and run used for its slope.
cpa.answer: Straight line through (0, 1) and (3, 7), rise 6 m and run 3 s; positive slope.
cpa.reference:
v_avg = Δx/Δt; average speed = distance/Δt.
Δ means change; Δt is elapsed time. Position-time slope gives velocity.
cpa.worked: A cart moves from 1 m to 7 m in 3 s at steady velocity. The position-time slope is (7-1)/3=2 m/s.

cpa.title: Read the motion picture
cpa.prompt: The graph shows a cart moving right. Read its position at 0 s and 3 s. Draw an arrow showing its direction.
cpa.answer: x(0)=1 m and x(3)=7 m; motion is right/positive.

cpa.title: Find the rate
cpa.prompt: Use the graph in 3. Position change = ____ - ____ = ____ m. Time = ____ s. Velocity = ____ m/s to the ____.
cpa.answer: 7-1=6 m; 3 s; +2 m/s/right.

cpa.title: A pause
cpa.prompt: A position-time graph stays at 5 m from 4 s to 6 s. Is the cart moving? Explain what stays the same.
cpa.answer: No. Position stays 5 m, so displacement is zero and velocity is zero.
cpa.frame: The cart is ____ because its position ____.

cpa.title: Draw a walk with a pause
cpa.prompt: Plot the supplied points and connect neighbors with straight lines. Label moving right, stopped, and moving left. Use the blank graph.
cpa.answer: 0-2 s: right at 2 m/s; 2-4 s: stopped; 4-6 s: left at 2 m/s. Points (0, 1),(2, 5),(4, 5),(6, 1).

cpa.title: Distance or displacement?
cpa.prompt: For the walk in 6, find distance traveled and displacement. Why is average velocity zero even though the person walked?
cpa.answer: Distance 4+4=8 m; displacement 0 m. Average velocity uses displacement; the walker returns to the start.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: Start at 4 m, move to 12 m, then finish at 6 m. Draw the route. Find distance, displacement with direction and final position.
cpa.answer: Distance 14 m; displacement +2 m (right); final position 6 m.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: A cart goes from 9 m to 3 m in 5 s at steady velocity. Find the velocity with direction. Sketch the shape of its position-time graph.
cpa.answer: 6 m left in 3 s = 2 m/s left, or -2 m/s with right positive. Straight descending line from (0, 9) to (3, 3).

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Draw two straight position-time graphs with different starting positions but the same velocity of 2 m/s. Explain the feature they share.
cpa.answer: Any two parallel lines with slope 2 m/s; vertical intercepts differ.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: East is positive. Start at 5 m, go to -3 m, then finish at 2 m. Sketch the route; calculate distance and displacement. Distinguish both from final position.
honors.answer: Distance 13 m; displacement -3 m; final position +2 m.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Sketch the graph through the two points. Draw and label the rise and run used for its slope.
honors.answer: Straight line through (0, 1) and (3, 7), rise 6 m and run 3 s; positive slope.
honors.reference:
v_avg = Δx/Δt; average speed = distance/Δt.
Δ means change; Δt is elapsed time. Position-time slope gives velocity.
honors.worked: A cart moves from 1 m to 7 m in 3 s at steady velocity. The position-time slope is (7-1)/3=2 m/s.

honors.title: Interpret all three intervals
honors.prompt: For the displayed position-time graph, calculate velocity on each segment. Label the direction of motion on each.

honors.title: Compare two averages
honors.prompt: For the full 6 s trip in 3, calculate average speed and average velocity. Explain their difference using the route.
honors.answer: Distance 4+6=10 m; average speed 10/6=1.67 m/s. Displacement 0-2=-2 m; average velocity -0.333 m/s.

honors.title: A line that misses the origin
honors.prompt: A straight graph passes through (2 s, 14 m) and (6 s, 6 m). Calculate slope, write x(t), and predict x at 9 s.
honors.answer: v=-2 m/s; x=18-2 t (m, s); x(9)=0 m, assuming the same line continues.

honors.title: Construct the graph
honors.prompt: Start at -2 m. Move at +3 m/s for 2 s, rest for 2 s, then move at -2 m/s for 3 s. Draw a labeled position-time graph; use additional graph paper if needed.
honors.answer: Vertices (0,-2),(2, 4),(4, 4),(7,-2). Net displacement zero; slope signs match each interval.

honors.title: Separate height and slope
honors.prompt: A student reads a point at (5 s, 10 m) and reports a velocity of 2 m/s. Under what additional condition would that calculation be justified?
honors.answer: It gives average velocity over 0-5 s if x(0)=0 m. It is also instantaneous velocity at 5 s only if the appropriate local slope is 2 m/s, e.g. a straight line from the origin. A single point is insufficient.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: East is positive. Start at -3 m, go to 5 m, then finish at -2 m. Sketch the route; calculate distance and displacement. Distinguish both from final position.
honors.answer: Distance 15 m; displacement +1 m; final position -2 m.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: A straight segment runs from (1 s, -2 m) to (5 s, +6 m). Find velocity and state what the slope units mean. Predict x at 7 s if the same motion continues.
honors.answer: v=8/4=+2 m/s; position increases by 2 m per second. x(7)=10 m.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: Two carts follow x_A=1+2 t and x_B=9-t, in meters and seconds. Sketch both graphs and find when and where they meet.
honors.answer: 1+2 t=9-t gives t=8/3 s and x=19/3 m. Intersection represents same place and time.

criteria: Read positions and elapsed times from a graph.
Find velocity from position change divided by time.
Explain the difference between speed and velocity.

title: Velocity graphs and components
target: Read a velocity graph and describe motion in two directions.
cpa_model: A flat velocity graph can show steady motion. At 2 m/s for 3 s, displacement = 2 × 3 = 6 m. For a diagonal arrow, count the horizontal and vertical changes separately.
honors_model: Signed area under v(t) gives displacement; total absolute area gives distance. For an angle θ measured from +x: v_x = v cos θ, v_y = v sin θ. State the reference axis and use degree mode.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A cart is at 4, 10, 16 m at 0, 1, 2 s. Predict its position at 8 s. State an assumption and a measurement that could challenge it.
cpa.answer: 52 m if the 6 m/s rightward motion continues. Check a later timed position against the prediction.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Sketch this graph. Shade the area and label the units that multiply to meters.
cpa.answer: Rectangle height 3 m/s, width 2 s; area 6 m east.
cpa.reference:
Δx = v_x Δt; Δy = v_y Δt.
For constant components. Subscripts x and y name the horizontal and vertical directions. Signed velocity-time area gives displacement.
cpa.worked: A cart travels at 3 m/s east for 2 s. The rectangle under its velocity-time graph has area 3×2=6 m, its displacement.

cpa.title: Steady does not mean stopped
cpa.prompt: Read the velocity graph. Circle the motion: stopped / steady motion / speeding up. Find the displacement in 6 s.
cpa.answer: Steady motion at +3 m/s; displacement +12 m.

cpa.title: Move, then wait
cpa.prompt: A cart moves west at 2 m/s for 3 s and then waits for 2 s. How far west is it from the start? Do the waiting seconds undo the trip?
cpa.answer: 6 m west; waiting adds zero displacement and does not undo the trip.

cpa.title: One diagonal motion
cpa.prompt: A drone moves 4 m east and 3 m north each second at the same time. Write its eastward and northward velocity components. Does it first go east, then north?
cpa.answer: 4 m/s east and 3 m/s north. Both components occur simultaneously; the actual motion is diagonal.

cpa.title: Make the components visible
cpa.prompt: From the start dot, draw an arrow ending 3 squares east and 2 north. One square represents 1 m/s. Label both component sizes.
cpa.answer: Diagonal from (0, 0) to (3, 2); components 3 m/s east and 2 m/s north.

cpa.title: Fix the speed claim
cpa.prompt: For a velocity with components 4 m/s east and 3 m/s north, the diagonal speed is given as 5 m/s. A student says it is 7 m/s. Explain using a sketch.
cpa.answer: Components are perpendicular, not along one line. The diagonal is 5 m/s as supplied; 4+3 is not its magnitude. No square-root calculation required.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A cart goes from 15 m to 5 m in 3 s at steady velocity. Find velocity and sketch its position-time graph.
cpa.answer: v=(5-15)/3=-3.333 m/s, left. Straight descending graph between the stated endpoints.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: A velocity graph stays at -2 m/s for 5 s. Give displacement with direction. A different object has components 2 m/s east and 1 m/s south: sketch its motion direction.
cpa.answer: Displacement -10 m, or 10 m in the negative direction. Second sketch points southeast, with east component twice the south component.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Draw a four-second velocity-time graph with nonzero motion but zero displacement. Give its distance traveled.
cpa.answer: Example +2 m/s for 2 s then -2 m/s for 2 s: areas cancel, distance 8 m.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: Positions are 18, 12, 6 m at 0, 2, 4 s. Predict position at 8 s. Give the rate, an assumption and a future test.
honors.answer: v=-3 m/s; x(8)=-6 m. Assumes constant velocity; compare another timed position with its uncertainty.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Sketch this graph. Shade the area and label the units that multiply to meters.
honors.answer: Rectangle height 3 m/s, width 2 s; area 6 m east.
honors.reference:
v_x = v cos θ; v_y = v sin θ.
θ measured from +x; degree mode. Signed velocity-time area gives displacement; total absolute area gives distance.
honors.worked: A cart travels at 3 m/s east for 2 s. The rectangle under its velocity-time graph has area 3×2=6 m, its displacement.

honors.title: Add signed areas
honors.prompt: Use the graph. Find displacement and distance from 0 to 6 s. Describe the motion on each interval.
honors.answer: First 4 s: +12 m. Last 2 s: -4 m. Displacement +8 m; distance 16 m. Motion positive then negative.

honors.title: Resolve a northeast velocity
honors.prompt: A drone travels at 14 m/s, 35° north of east. Sketch the angle and calculate both components. Compare their sizes before calculating.
honors.answer: v_x=14 cos 35°=11.5 m/s; v_y=14 sin 35°=8.03 m/s. East component larger because the direction is closer to east.

honors.title: Change the reference axis
honors.prompt: A boat travels at 10 m/s, 20° west of north. With east +x and north +y, find the signed components. Explain your choice of sine and cosine.
honors.answer: v_x=-10 sin 20°=-3.42 m/s; v_y=10 cos 20°=9.40 m/s. North component is adjacent to the stated angle.

honors.title: Draw velocity and displacement
honors.prompt: An object has v=(+4,-3) m/s for 2 s. Draw the velocity vector and calculate its speed, displacement vector, and displacement magnitude.
honors.answer: Speed 5 m/s. Displacement (8,-6) m, magnitude 10 m, same southeast direction.

honors.title: Two horizontal graphs
honors.prompt: Explain the difference between a horizontal line at +5 on a position-time graph and a horizontal line at +5 on a velocity-time graph. Include units.
honors.answer: x=5 m: stationary at that position, v=0. v=5 m/s: constant positive motion with zero acceleration; position changes 5 m each second.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: A straight position-time segment goes from (1 s, -3 m) to (5 s, 17 m). Find velocity, interpret its units and predict x at 7 s if motion continues.
honors.answer: v=5 m/s; position increases 5 m each second. x(7)=27 m.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: A velocity graph stays at +2 m/s for 3 s, then -1 m/s for 2 s. Find displacement and distance. State the information needed to interpret a vector angle of 30°.
honors.answer: Displacement 6-2=4 m; distance 6+2=8 m. Need reference axis and direction/sense of angle.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: A cart moves at +4 m/s for 3 s, then -2 m/s. How long must the second interval last to return to its start? Sketch the graph and find average speed for the full trip.
honors.answer: Positive displacement 12 m; return takes 6 s. Distance 24 m in 9 s gives 8/3 m/s; average velocity zero.

criteria: Use signed velocity-time area to find displacement.
Represent horizontal and vertical components separately.
Distinguish graph height, slope and vector magnitude.

title: Predict a position and a range
target: Predict a future position and explain the limits of the prediction.
cpa_model: For steady motion: final position = starting position + velocity × time. Example: start 2 m; move 3 m/s right for 2 s. Change = 6 m, so final position = 8 m.
honors_model: Constant velocity: x_f = x_0 + vt. For independent bounded x_0 and v with exact positive t, a conservative coordinate half-width is δx = δx_0 + tδv. These bounds are not probabilities.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: Start at 5 m, move to 14 m, then finish at 7 m. Draw the route. Find distance, displacement with direction and final position.
cpa.answer: Distance 16 m; displacement +2 m (right); final position 7 m.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Mark the start, central endpoint and endpoint range on a number line. What assumption applies throughout the three seconds?
cpa.answer: Start 1 m, middle 7 m, range 4-10 m; constant velocity within the stated bounds.
cpa.reference:
x_f = x_i + vΔt.
Constant velocity; i = initial, f = final. Use the same units for all positions.
cpa.worked: A cart starts at 1 m and moves right at 2 m/s for 3 s. Central prediction: 1+2×3=7 m. If its speed could be 1 to 3 m/s, the endpoint range is 4 to 10 m.

cpa.title: Start plus change
cpa.prompt: A cart starts at 3 m and moves right at 2 m/s for 4 s. Find its displacement and final position. Mark the endpoint.
cpa.answer: Displacement 8 m right; final position 11 m.

cpa.title: Predict leftward motion
cpa.prompt: A cart starts at 12 m and moves left at 2 m/s for 3 s. Change = ____ m left. Final position = ____ m.
cpa.answer: 6 m left; 12-6=6 m.

cpa.title: Match the time units
cpa.prompt: A rover moves at 2 m/s for 1 minute. Use 1 minute = 60 seconds. Find its distance at this steady speed.
cpa.answer: 2×60=120 m. Must convert minutes to seconds before multiplying.

cpa.title: Read the range
cpa.prompt: A prediction is 10 m with a range from 8 m to 12 m. Label the middle, lower end, and upper end. Find how far each end is from the middle.
cpa.answer: Middle 10 m; lower 8 m; upper 12 m; half-width 2 m; full width 4 m.

cpa.title: A slow and a fast case
cpa.prompt: A cart starts at 0 m. Its steady speed could be as low as 1 m/s or as high as 3 m/s, all to the right. Find its possible position range after 4 s.
cpa.answer: Lower 1×4=4 m; upper 3×4=12 m. Range 4-12 m under the stated constant-speed bounds.
cpa.frame: Slow case: ____. Fast case: ____. My range is ____.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A velocity graph is constant at -3 m/s for 5 s. Find displacement. A second object has components 7 m/s east and 2 m/s south; sketch its direction.
cpa.answer: Displacement -15 m. Second arrow points southeast with component ratio 7: 2.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: A cart starts at 2 m and moves right at 3 m/s for 2 s. Find the central final position. If the possible final positions run from 7 to 9 m, state the range and one assumption.
cpa.answer: Central 8 m; range 7-9 m. Assumes steady velocity for the interval and the stated starting position/model.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Design two different starting-position and speed pairs that both give an endpoint of 10 m after 2 s. Draw the routes.
cpa.answer: Examples x 0=0 m, v=5 m/s and x 0=6 m, v=2 m/s; both endpoints 10 m.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: East is positive. Start at 6 m, go to -4 m, then finish at 3 m. Sketch the route; calculate distance and displacement. Distinguish both from final position.
honors.answer: Distance 17 m; displacement -3 m; final position +3 m.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Mark the start, central endpoint and endpoint range on a number line. What assumption applies throughout the three seconds?
honors.answer: Start 1 m, middle 7 m, range 4-10 m; constant velocity within the stated bounds.
honors.reference:
x_f = x_i + vt; δx_f = δx_i + tδv.
Constant velocity; exact positive t and independent bounded starting position/velocity. δ marks a half-width, not a probability.
honors.worked: A cart starts at 1 m and moves right at 2 m/s for 3 s. Central prediction: 1+2×3=7 m. If its speed could be 1 to 3 m/s, the endpoint range is 4 to 10 m.

honors.title: Units and a starting position
honors.prompt: A train starts at x=5 km and moves at +20 m/s for 2 minutes. Calculate displacement and final position in km.
honors.answer: t=120 s; displacement 2400 m=2.40 km; final position 7.40 km.

honors.title: Independent bounds
honors.prompt: x_0=10±1 m, v=2.0±0.2 m/s, t=5.0 s exact. Find central position, half-width, endpoints, and full width.
honors.answer: Central 20 m; half-width 1+5(0.2)=2 m; interval 18-22 m; full width 4 m.

honors.title: A negative velocity
honors.prompt: x_0=30±2 m, v=-3.0±0.1 m/s, t=10 s exact. Calculate the full position interval using extreme inputs.
honors.answer: Lower 28+(-3.1)(10)=-3 m; upper 32+(-2.9)(10)=3 m; central 0 m, half-width 3 m.

honors.title: Show how the bound grows
honors.prompt: For x_0=4±1 m and v=2±0.5 m/s, graph central, lower, and upper x(t) from 0 to 4 s. Label the endpoint range.
honors.answer: Central 4+2 t; lower 3+1.5 t; upper 5+2.5 t. At 4 s: central 12 m; range 9-15 m.

honors.title: Input uncertainty or model error?
honors.prompt: A precise speed measurement is used to predict an asteroid position with six months of constant velocity. Explain why tiny measurement bounds do not make the forecast exact.
honors.answer: Gravity changes velocity; Earth moves; 3 D geometry and other omitted effects matter. Narrow input bounds do not remove model error.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: Velocity is +3 m/s for 5 s, then -2 m/s for 3 s. Find displacement and distance. Explain the reference information needed for an angle of 25°.
honors.answer: Displacement 9 m; distance 21 m. An angle needs a reference direction/axis and rotation sense.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: x_0=-5±0.5 m, v=3.0±0.1 m/s, t=10 s exact. Give central final position, its interval, and the full width. Name an assumption.
honors.answer: Central 25 m; half-width 0.5+10(0.1)=1.5 m; interval 23.5-26.5 m; full width 3 m. Constant velocity and independent bounded inputs.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: Initial position is 2±0.5 m; constant velocity is 3±0.2 m/s; time is exactly 4 s. Find the central prediction and worst-case endpoint bounds.
honors.answer: Central 14 m; lower 1.5+2.8×4=12.7 m; upper 2.5+3.2×4=15.3 m. These are bounds, not probabilities.

criteria: Use matching units and include the starting position.
Report a central prediction and its bounds.
Distinguish a measurement range from model limitations.

title: Vector addition
target: Add displacement vectors and use a model to explain where an object ends up.
cpa_model: A resultant is one arrow from the first start to the final end. Slide arrows tip to tail without rotating them. Example: 3 m east + 2 m east = 5 m east. Opposite directions subtract.
honors_model: Use east = +x and north = +y. Add x and y separately. Magnitude = √(R_x² + R_y²). Find an angle from the component ratio and name its reference direction. Use degree mode.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A cart moves from 0 m to 8 m east in 4 s at a steady pace. Find its speed. Draw a velocity arrow showing its direction. Explain what the arrow tells you that speed alone does not.
cpa.answer: Speed 2 m/s; velocity arrow points east. Speed supplies magnitude only; velocity also supplies direction.
cpa.diagnostic: Look for units and an explicit direction, not an unlabeled arrow.

cpa.title: Read and explain a worked model
cpa.prompt: A walker goes 3 m east, then 4 m north. A resultant is one arrow from the original start to the final endpoint.
cpa.answer: Start (0, 0), turn (3, 0), finish (3, 4). Distance 7 m; displacement 5 m northeast. The resultant joins the original start to the final endpoint.
cpa.diagnostic: If the student says 7 m northeast, ask which line is being measured.
cpa.reference:
R_x = A_x + B_x; R_y = A_y + B_y.
Use east = +x and north = +y. Add signed components; draw R from the original start to the final endpoint.

cpa.title: Finish the model
cpa.prompt: Walk 4 m east, then 3 m north. The first arrow is drawn. Add the second arrow from its tip and a dashed resultant from the original start.
cpa.answer: Route (0, 0) to (4, 0) to (4, 3); R ends at (4, 3). Components 4 m east, 3 m north. Distance 7 m; displacement 5 m northeast.
cpa.diagnostic: Second arrow must start at the first tip; no rotation or rescaling.

cpa.title: A trip that doubles back
cpa.prompt: Walk 6 m east, then 4 m west. Draw and label the route and resultant. Give distance and displacement. Explain which length follows the path.
cpa.answer: Distance 10 m. Displacement 2 m east. The second leg cancels 4 m of eastward displacement but still adds 4 m of path length.
cpa.diagnostic: A negative result may reveal subtracting larger from smaller without first choosing a direction.

cpa.title: Use a new scale
cpa.prompt: Walk 6 m east, then 8 m north. Draw both arrows and the resultant. Give distance and displacement. The straight-line length is supplied: 10 m.
cpa.answer: Distance 14 m; displacement 10 m northeast. Components 6 m east and 8 m north. R is the diagonal from the original start.
cpa.diagnostic: Exact angle and use of the Pythagorean theorem are not required in CPA.

cpa.title: Add two diagonal arrows
cpa.prompt: A: 5 m east and 2 m north. B: 3 m west and 1 m north. A is drawn. Add B and R. State each net component and the general compass direction.
cpa.answer: Route (0, 0) to (5, 2) to (2, 3). Net 2 m east and 3 m north; northeast.
cpa.diagnostic: Check B travels left and upward from A’s tip. Do not require a magnitude calculation.

cpa.title: Predict, draw, check
cpa.prompt: Walk 3 m east, 4 m north, then 3 m west. Predict what cancels. Draw the route and R. Give distance and displacement. Check your prediction against the model.
cpa.answer: East-west components cancel. Route distance 10 m; displacement 4 m north.
cpa.diagnostic: If the student reports zero displacement, ask what happened to the northward leg.

cpa.title: Find and repair the mistake
cpa.prompt: Sam adds 4 m east and 3 m north. His dashed R is wrong. Explain why and draw the correct route and resultant on the empty grid.
cpa.answer: Sam connects the two tips; that arrow is not the combined start-to-finish displacement. Correct route: (0, 0) to (4, 0) to (4, 3); R = (4, 3) m.
cpa.diagnostic: A valid repair may also use a correctly constructed parallelogram. Accept an explanation of the endpoints.

cpa.title: One trip, three questions
cpa.prompt:
A student walks 6 m east in 6 s, then 8 m north in 8 s. The direct start-to-finish length is 10 m. For each answer, decide whether to use path length or the start-to-finish arrow, then solve:
(a) Distance walked? (b) Displacement?
(c) Average speed for the whole trip?
cpa.answer: (a) Path: 14 m. (b) Endpoints: 10 m northeast. (c) Path and total time: 14 m / 14 s = 1 m/s.
cpa.diagnostic: Do not use 10 m to calculate average speed. That quantity is relevant to average-velocity magnitude.

cpa.title: Exit check - work independently
cpa.prompt: A goes 4 m east and 1 m north. B goes 1 m west and 3 m north. Draw tip to tail and add R. Give both net components and a general compass direction. Explain one check of your model.
cpa.answer: Route (0, 0) to (4, 1) to (3, 4). Net 3 m east, 4 m north; northeast. Check endpoint or compare signed component sums with the sketch.
cpa.diagnostic: Optional magnitude 5 m is correct but not required by this prompt.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Design two routes
cpa.prompt: Finish 4 m east and 3 m north of your start. Design one route of length 7 m and another of length 11 m. Use only north, south, east or west legs. Label all lengths and draw each resultant.
cpa.answer: One route: 4 m east, 3 m north (7 m). Another: 6 m east, 3 m north, 2 m west (11 m). Both end at (4, 3); both have displacement 5 m northeast.
cpa.diagnostic: Many routes work. Require both endpoint and total-length checks.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Explore the limits
cpa.prompt: Point two 5 m displacement arrows in any directions. Draw the smallest and largest possible resultants, then one between those extremes. Estimate the intermediate resultant and explain why your limits make sense.
cpa.answer: Minimum 0 m for opposite directions; maximum 10 m for the same direction. A perpendicular pair gives about 7.1 m; many intermediate examples work.
cpa.diagnostic: Opposite equal vectors return to the start. Intermediate magnitude estimates should agree with the drawn scale.

honors.title: Retrieve and distinguish
honors.prompt: A cart moves from 0 m to +6 m in 3 s, then to +2 m in 2 s. Find average speed and average velocity for the full trip. Sketch the route and explain why the answers differ.
honors.answer: Path 6 + 4 = 10 m in 5 s: average speed 2 m/s. Displacement +2 m: average velocity +0.40 m/s (east).
honors.diagnostic: Distance counts both legs; displacement accounts for the westward return.

honors.title: Explain a worked model
honors.prompt: Find B’s westward component. Explain why R begins at the original start.
honors.answer: R = (3, 4) m, 5 m at 53.1° north of east. B runs from (4, 1) to (3, 4), so its x component is negative.
honors.diagnostic: A correct angle is steeper than 45° because the north component exceeds the east component.
honors.worked:
East=+x; north=+y. R_x=4-1=3 m;
R_y=1+3=4 m; R=√(3²+4²)=5 m.
θ=tan⁻¹(4/3)=53.1° north of east.
honors.reference: R = √(R_x² + R_y²).

honors.title: Complete, then check
honors.prompt: A=(6, 2) m; B=(-4, 3) m. A is drawn. Add B and R tip to tail; find R’s components, magnitude and direction. Check the quadrant.
honors.answer: R = (2, 5) m; √29 = 5.39 m at 68.2° north of east.
honors.diagnostic: Accept 21.8° east of north with a correctly labeled reference.

honors.title: A different quadrant
honors.prompt: A = (2, -5) m and B = (-6, 2) m. Predict the resultant quadrant. Draw tip to tail; calculate the components, magnitude and direction. State how you know your angle is in the correct quadrant.
honors.answer: R = (-4,-3) m; 5 m at 36.9° south of west, or 216.9° counterclockwise from +x.
honors.diagnostic: An isolated tan⁻¹(3/4) value is insufficient without its quadrant.

honors.title: Choose the correct component signs
honors.prompt:
A is 10 m at 30° north of east: Ax = 10 cos 30° = 8.66 m and Ay = 10 sin 30° = 5.00 m.
B is 6 m at 60° north of west. Sketch both arrows, resolve B into signed components, and find the resultant magnitude and direction.
honors.diagnostic: Angle from west makes the westward cosine component negative. Use degree mode.

honors.title: The angle is measured from north
honors.prompt: Walk 12 m at 25° east of north, then 7 m west. Sketch first and predict the resultant quadrant. Calculate components, magnitude and direction. Explain which component uses cosine and why.
honors.diagnostic: The north component is adjacent to the given 25° angle, so it uses cosine.

honors.title: Plan the direct return
honors.prompt: A survey team walks 8 m east, 5 m north, then 2 m west. A clear field allows a straight return to the start. Find the route distance before returning and the direct return displacement, including magnitude and direction. Draw both the outward route and the return.
honors.answer: Outward path distance 15 m. Final position (6, 5) m. Direct return (-6,-5) m; √61 = 7.81 m at 39.8° south of west.
honors.diagnostic: Do not report the outward resultant direction as the return direction.

honors.title: Diagnose the reasoning
honors.prompt: A student adds 10 m east and 10 m at 60° north of east using √(10² + 10²) = 14.1 m. Identify the violated condition. Draw a correct model and use it to repair the solution, including direction.
honors.answer: The two original vectors are not perpendicular. R = (15, 8.660) m; √300 = 17.32 m at 30.0° north of east.
honors.diagnostic: The Pythagorean theorem applies to perpendicular components, not arbitrary vector magnitudes.

honors.title: Represent one trip in several ways
honors.prompt:
A robot moves steadily from (0, 0) m to (6, 0) m in 3 s, then steadily to (6, 8) m in another 4 s.
(a) Draw the path and resultant; find distance and displacement.
(b) Find average speed and the average-velocity vector for the full trip.
(c) Sketch x-versus-time and y-versus-time graphs. Explain how each graph records the same motion as your path diagram.
honors.answer: Distance 14 m; displacement (6, 8) m = 10 m at 53.1° north of east. Average speed 2 m/s. Average velocity (6/7, 8/7) m/s, magnitude 10/7 = 1.43 m/s in the displacement direction. x(t) = 2 t for 0-3 s, then 6 m. y(t) = 0 for 0-3 s, then 2(t-3) for 3-7 s.
honors.diagnostic: The graph slopes give component velocities; start/end changes give the displacement components.

honors.title: Exit check - solve without the worked model
honors.prompt: A = (4, -3) m and B = (-1, 5) m. Find R, its magnitude and direction. Choose C so A + B + C = 0. Draw a closed tip-to-tail route and give one physical or mathematical check of your answer.
honors.answer: R = (3, 2) m; √13 = 3.61 m at 33.7° north of east. C = (-3,-2) m. Tip-to-tail route: (0, 0) to (4,-3) to (3, 2) to (0, 0).
honors.diagnostic: Require route closure or both sums equal to zero; a numerical answer alone is weak evidence.

honors.title: STRETCH: Missing direction
honors.prompt: The first displacement is 6 m east. The second has magnitude 10 m. Finish directly north of the start. Find the second vector’s components and direction, and the resultant. Draw the model. Explain whether more than one solution meets the north requirement.
honors.answer: B<sub>x</sub> = -6 m. B<sub>y</sub> = +√(100-36) = +8 m. B is 10 m at 53.1° north of west; R is 8 m north.
honors.diagnostic: The negative square-root branch ends south, so it violates the stated requirement.

honors.title: STRETCH: Decide what is possible
honors.prompt: Two displacements have magnitudes 5 m and 3 m. Test whether resultants of 1 m, 6 m and 9 m are possible using limits. Draw the 6 m case to scale. Estimate the angle between the original arrows with tails together. Explain why the tip-to-tail triangle uses a different interior angle. Optional: derive an angle-resultant relationship to check your drawing.
honors.answer: Allowed magnitude range is 2-8 m. Thus 1 m and 9 m are impossible; 6 m is possible. For included angle θ: 6² = 5² + 3² + 2(5)(3) cos θ, so θ ≈ 86.2°. The tip-to-tail triangle has supplementary interior angle ≈ 93.8°.
honors.diagnostic: Mirrored arrangements give the same magnitude. A scale estimate near 86° is sufficient unless the optional derivation is assigned.

criteria: Place arrows tip to tail without rotating them.
Combine east-west and north-south components separately.
State the resultant with units and a clear direction.

cpa: Draw and label arrows tip to tail; keep their length and direction.
Draw the resultant from the original start to the final endpoint.
State net east-west and north-south motion with units and direction.
honors: Connect tip-to-tail diagrams to signed component sums.
Give magnitude, units and an angle with a named reference direction.
Check the result against the diagram, limits and physical situation.

title: Changing velocity
target: Calculate acceleration and distinguish speeding up, slowing down, and turning.
cpa_model: Acceleration = velocity change ÷ time. Example: 2 to 8 m/s in 3 s gives (8-2)÷3=2 m/s². Acceleration changes velocity; turning changes velocity even at steady speed.
honors_model: Average acceleration = (v_f-v_i)/Δt. Speed increases when velocity and acceleration point the same way. Opposite directions mean slowing. Zero velocity at an instant does not guarantee zero acceleration.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A velocity graph is constant at -4 m/s for 6 s. Find displacement. A second object has components 8 m/s east and 3 m/s south; sketch its direction.
cpa.answer: Displacement -24 m. Second arrow points southeast with component ratio 8: 3.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw initial and final velocity arrows and one acceleration arrow. Use arrow lengths to show the speed change.
cpa.answer: Both velocity arrows east, final one shorter; acceleration west.
cpa.reference:
a_avg = (v_f - v_i)/Δt.
i = initial; f = final. Compare directions of velocity and acceleration to decide whether speed increases.
cpa.worked: A cart moving east slows from 8 to 2 m/s in 3 s. Taking east positive, a=(2-8)/3=-2 m/s². It keeps moving east while acceleration points west.

cpa.title: Watch velocity grow
cpa.prompt: Read the graph. Find velocity change over 3 s, then acceleration. Is the cart speeding up?
cpa.answer: 8-2=6 m/s; 6/3=2 m/s²; speeding up.

cpa.title: A bike slows
cpa.prompt: A bike moving east slows from 10 m/s to 4 m/s in 5 s. How much speed is lost each second? Which way does acceleration point?
cpa.answer: Loses 6/5=1.2 m/s each second; acceleration 1.2 m/s² west, opposite motion.
cpa.frame: Step 1: Find the speed lost: 10 - 4. Step 2: Divide by 5 s. Step 3: Acceleration points opposite the bike’s motion while it slows.

cpa.title: A turn at steady speed
cpa.prompt: A toy car moves around a circle at steady speed. Does it accelerate? Draw velocity arrows at two points to support your answer.
cpa.answer: Yes. Tangent velocity directions change, so velocity changes.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A goes 5 m east and 3 m north. B then goes 2 m west and 7 m south. Draw the route and find the endpoint relative to the start.
cpa.answer: 3 m east and 4 m south. Add each pair of signed components.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: A cart moves west at 6 m/s, then west at 2 m/s two seconds later. Is it speeding up or slowing down? Find the acceleration direction and magnitude.
cpa.answer: Slowing down; velocity changes 4 m/s east over 2 s, so 2 m/s² east.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Make a velocity-time graph of a cart speeding up westward from 1 to 5 m/s in 2 s. Use east as positive and explain the acceleration sign.
cpa.answer: Graph from -1 to -5 m/s; slope -2 m/s². Speed increases although acceleration is negative.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: Velocity is +4 m/s for 6 s, then -3 m/s for 4 s. Find displacement and distance. Explain the reference information needed for an angle of 30°.
honors.answer: Displacement 12 m; distance 36 m. An angle needs a reference direction/axis and rotation sense.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Draw initial and final velocity arrows and one acceleration arrow. Use arrow lengths to show the speed change.
honors.answer: Both velocity arrows east, final one shorter; acceleration west.
honors.reference:
a_avg = (v_f - v_i)/Δt.
i = initial; f = final. Compare directions of velocity and acceleration to decide whether speed increases.
honors.worked: A cart moving east slows from 8 to 2 m/s in 3 s. Taking east positive, a=(2-8)/3=-2 m/s². It keeps moving east while acceleration points west.

honors.title: Signed acceleration
honors.prompt: Use the graph to calculate acceleration and explain the speed trend. State when the cart is momentarily at rest.
honors.answer: a=(4-(-8))/3=+4 m/s²; slows untilt=2 s, rests instantaneously, then speeds up positive.

honors.title: Braking intervals
honors.prompt:
A car travels at +24 m/s and slows at a constant rate to 0 m/s in 7.0 s. The positive direction is the car’s original direction of travel.
(a) Calculate its acceleration.
(b) Calculate its displacement during braking.
(c) Explain the sign of each answer.
honors.answer: (a) a = (0 - 24)/4.0 = -6.0 m/s². (b) Average velocity = (24 + 0)/2 = 12 m/s; displacement = 12 × 4.0 = +48 m. (c) Acceleration is opposite the positive motion, so it is negative. The car keeps moving forward while braking, so displacement is positive.

honors.title: Small acceleration, long time
honors.prompt: A hypothetical constant sideways acceleration is 2×10⁻⁶ m/s² for 10⁶ s. Find Δv and explain why small acceleration alone cannot justify ignoring it.
honors.answer: Δv=2 m/s. Accumulated change depends on time; this is a hypothetical comparison, not a real asteroid forecast.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: A=(5, -3) m and B=(-3, 7) m. Find R, magnitude and direction. Choose C so A+B+C=0 and sketch the route.
honors.answer: R=(2, 4) m; magnitude ≈4.472 m at 63.43° north of east. C=(-2, -4) m.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: Velocity changes from-3 to-9 m/s in 4 s, then stays-9 m/s for 4 s. Find acceleration and speed trend in each interval.
honors.answer: First-3 m/s², speeding up. Then 0 m/s², constant speed 9 m/s.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: A cart begins at -6 m/s and has constant acceleration +2 m/s² for 5 s. Sketch v versus t; find turning time, displacement and distance.
honors.answer: Turns at 3 s. Displacement -30+25=-5 m. Distance 9 m west plus 4 m east=13 m.

criteria: Calculate acceleration from velocity change and time.
Compare acceleration direction with velocity direction.
Explain why turning at steady speed is acceleration.

title: Choose a motion method
target: Choose a motion relationship and justify its assumptions.
cpa_model: Steady velocity: change in position = v×t. Constant acceleration: final velocity = start velocity + a×t. If acceleration is constant, average velocity = (start + final velocity)÷2.
honors_model: For constant acceleration: v_f=v_i+at; Δx=v_i t+½at²; v_f²=v_i²+2 aΔx. Choose an equation containing the knowns and the unknown. State the modeled interval.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A cart starts at 3 m and moves right at 5 m/s for 2 s. Predict final position. Allowed endpoints are 11 to 15 m; state this interval and one assumption.
cpa.answer: Central position 13 m; interval 11-15 m. Assumes steady velocity and the stated start.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Show the same 9 m using the area of a triangle on a velocity-time graph.
cpa.answer: Triangle base 3 s, height 6 m/s; area half of 18=9 m.
cpa.reference:
v_f = v_i + aΔt; Δx = ½(v_i + v_f)Δt.
Constant acceleration; i = initial, f = final. At constant velocity, Δx = vΔt.
cpa.worked: From rest, a cart accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 3 s. Final velocity=6 m/s; average velocity=(0+6)/2=3 m/s; displacement=3×3=9 m.

cpa.title: Choose the relationship
cpa.prompt: A cart moves steadily at 3 m/s for 4 s. Which relationship fits: steady velocity or changing velocity? Find displacement.
cpa.answer: Steady velocity; 3×4=12 m.

cpa.title: Build final velocity
cpa.prompt: A cart starts at 2 m/s east. It gains 2 m/s each second for 3 s. Complete: gain=2×3=____ m/s; final=2+____=____ m/s east.
cpa.answer: Gain 6 m/s; final 8 m/s east.

cpa.title: Find the distance while speeding up
cpa.prompt: Use the cart in 4. Its acceleration is constant. Average velocity=(2+8)÷2=____ m/s. Displacement=average velocity×3 s=____ m.
cpa.answer: Average 5 m/s east; displacement 15 m east.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A cart travels west at 10 m/s and west at 3 m/s 2 s later. Is it speeding up? Find acceleration size and direction.
cpa.answer: Slowing down; change is 7 m/s east. Acceleration 3.5 m/s² east.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: A cart speeds up uniformly from 0 to 6 m/s east in 5 s. Find acceleration, average velocity and displacement. Show each step.
cpa.answer: a=2 m/s² east; average 3 m/s east; displacement 9 m east.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way

title: Inertia and balanced forces
target: Predict motion when the net force is zero.
cpa_model: Zero net force means no change in velocity. A resting object stays at rest; a moving object keeps the same speed and direction. Example: 8 N right and 8 N left balance, even if the box is moving.
honors_model: Newton’s first law concerns net external force in an inertial frame. ΣF=0 implies a=0 and constant velocity. Forces may still act and cancel. Velocity and force are different physical quantities.

ΣF = 0 ⇒ a = 0 ⇒ v = constant.
ΣF means net force. Balanced forces allow rest or steady motion in a straight line.

cpa.answer: 12-4=8 N right; 8/4=2 m/s² right.

visual.caption: The dot represents the object. Mass: 4 kg

cpa.title: Balanced but moving
cpa.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves left with 5 N right and 5 N left. Find a. Describe its next motion in this ideal model.
cpa.answer: Net 0 N; a 0; keeps same leftward velocity.

cpa.title: Compare two masses
cpa.prompt: The same 6 N net force acts on 2 kg and 3 kg carts. Find both accelerations. Which changes velocity more quickly?
cpa.answer: 3 m/s² and 2 m/s²; 2 kg cart.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A cart is at 5, 12, 19 m at 0, 1, 2 s. Predict its position at 9 s. State an assumption and a measurement that could challenge it.
cpa.answer: 68 m if the 7 m/s rightward motion continues. Check a later timed position against the prediction.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: An 8 kg object has 50 N right and 18 N left. Draw the forces, calculate net force, and find a with direction.
cpa.answer: 32 N right; 4 m/s² right.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Find two different pairs of opposite horizontal forces that give the same 6 N net force right. Keep mass 2 kg and compare accelerations.
cpa.answer: Examples 8 and 2 N; 11 and 5 N. Both give 3 m/s² right.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: A 4 kg object hangs still from a vertical string. Use g=9.8 N/kg. Name all forces on it with sources, sizes and directions. Does object-on-string belong on this diagram?
honors.answer: Weight 39.2 N down from Earth and tension 39.2 N up from string. Object-on-string acts on the string, not the object.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Draw arrows for both forces, then a separate net-force arrow. Explain why 9/2 is not the acceleration.
honors.answer: Net arrow 6 N right; 9 N omits the opposing force.
honors.reference:
ΣF = ma; a = ΣF/m.
Add signed forces on the same object before dividing by mass. N/kg = m/s².
honors.worked: A 2 kg cart has 9 N right and 3 N left. Net force=6 N right; a=6/2=3 m/s² right. Add forces before dividing by mass.

honors.title: Work from force arrows
honors.prompt: A 5 kg object has 32 N right and 12 N left. It currently moves left at 6 m/s. Find a and v after 1 s under constant forces.
honors.answer: Net 20 N right; a 4 m/s² right; v=-6+4=-2 m/s(left), slowing.

visual.caption: The dot represents the object. Mass: 5 kg; velocity left

honors.title: Find an unknown force
honors.prompt: A 3 kg cart accelerates at-2 m/s². It has 4 N right and an unknown leftward force. Find that force magnitude.

honors.title: From braking to force
honors.prompt: A 1500 kg car slows uniformly from 30 m/s to rest in 5 s. Find acceleration and net force. State your positive direction.
honors.answer: Forward positive; a=-6 m/s²; F=-9000 N.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: Positions are 21, 14, 7 m at 0, 2, 4 s. Predict position at 9 s. Give the rate, an assumption and a future test.
honors.answer: v=-3.5 m/s; x(9)=-10.5 m. Assumes constant velocity; compare another timed position with its uncertainty.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: A 4 kg cart has 7 N right and 19 N left. Find a. Is it necessarily moving left? Name the information needed to determine whether it speeds up.
honors.answer: Net-12 N; a=-3 m/s². Need current velocity; leftward motion speeds up, rightward motion slows.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: A 3 kg cart accelerates left at 2 m/s². A rope pulls right with 10 N. Find the other horizontal force. Can the cart be moving right at this instant?
honors.answer: Net -6 N means other force -16 N. It can be moving right and slowing.

criteria: Find net force before dividing by mass.
State acceleration with units and direction.
Separate acceleration direction from motion direction.

title: Forces on two objects
target: Identify an equal-and-opposite interaction pair on different objects.
cpa_model: An interaction pair has two objects: hand on wall; wall on hand. The forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, but they act on different objects.
honors_model: Newton’s third law: F_A on B=-F_B on A at the same instant. Pair forces act on different objects; their accelerations can differ because a=F/m. Do not combine forces from different free-body diagrams.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: With a fixed net force, a 4 kg system accelerates at 12 m/s². Predict acceleration for a 8 kg system. State a control needed for this comparison.
cpa.answer: 6 m/s²; the mass doubles at the same net force. Keep the net force fixed, including resistance.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw separate force diagrams for the horizontal interaction. Explain why equal forces do not imply equal accelerations.
cpa.answer: Equal opposite interaction arrows on different bodies; acceleration also depends on mass.
cpa.reference:
FA on B = -FB on A.
The two forces act on different objects at the same instant. Their accelerations can differ.
cpa.worked: Two skaters push apart. Each feels 20 N from the other. If their masses are 40 and 80 kg, accelerations are 0.5 and 0.25 m/s² in opposite directions.

cpa.title: Name both forces
cpa.prompt: A hand pushes a wall to the right. Complete both statements: hand on____ pushes right;____ on hand pushes left.
cpa.answer: Hand on wall; wall on hand. Equal forces on different objects.

cpa.title: Heavy and light carts
cpa.prompt: A heavy cart and light cart push apart. Compare the force sizes. Which has the greater acceleration from this interaction, and why?
cpa.answer: Equal forces; lighter cart greater acceleration for same force.

cpa.title: Balanced or a pair?
cpa.prompt: A book rests on a table. Earth pulls book down; table pushes book up. Are these the two forces of one interaction pair? Explain by naming the object receiving each.
cpa.answer: No; both act on book. Actual partners are book on Earth and book on table.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: Start at 6 m, move to 16 m, then finish at 8 m. Draw the route. Find distance, displacement with direction and final position.
cpa.answer: Distance 18 m; displacement +2 m (right); final position 8 m.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: Afoot pushes ground backward. Name the partner force and the object it acts on. Explain how this can help the person move forward.
cpa.answer: Ground pushes foot forward; acts on foot. Forward external force can accelerate person.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Choose two masses that would give a 3: 1 acceleration ratio while the forces remain equal. Explain which skater accelerates more.
cpa.answer: Any inverse mass ratio, e.g. 20 and 60 kg; lighter skater accelerates three times as much.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: A 0.4 kg system accelerates at 0.6 m/s². Predict acceleration for 0.8 kg at the same net force. Explain the effect of greater resistance.
honors.answer: Net force 0.24 N; new a≈0.3 m/s². Extra resistance reduces net force and acceleration if driving force is unchanged.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Draw separate force diagrams for the horizontal interaction. Explain why equal forces do not imply equal accelerations.
honors.answer: Equal opposite interaction arrows on different bodies; acceleration also depends on mass.
honors.reference:
FA on B = -FB on A.
The two forces act on different objects at the same instant. Their accelerations can differ.
honors.worked: Two skaters push apart. Each feels 20 N from the other. If their masses are 40 and 80 kg, accelerations are 0.5 and 0.25 m/s² in opposite directions.

honors.title: Equal forces, different results
honors.prompt: Cart A is 1 kg and cart B is 4 kg. During an ideal horizontal interaction, each force magnitude is 12 N. Find both acceleration magnitudes and compare them.
honors.answer: aA 12 m/s²; aB 3 m/s²; opposite directions.

honors.title: Identify actual partners
honors.prompt: For a book on a table, name the partner of Earth-on-book and the partner of table-on-book. Explain why weight and normal are not a third-law pair.
honors.answer: Book-on-Earth and book-on-table. Weight and normal both act on book; pair forces act on different objects.

honors.title: Horse plus cart
honors.prompt: The horse pulls cart forward and cart pulls horse backward equally. Draw a system boundary around both and explain how the system can accelerate forward.
honors.answer: Internal horse cart forces cancel in total; external ground force on horse can exceed resistance. Need net external force.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: East is positive. Start at 7 m, go to -5 m, then finish at 4 m. Sketch the route; calculate distance and displacement. Distinguish both from final position.
honors.answer: Distance 21 m; displacement -3 m; final position +4 m.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: A spacecraft pushes on a massive asteroid. Compare instantaneous interaction forces and accelerations from the interaction. State an assumption in your acceleration comparison.
honors.answer: Equal opposite forces; smaller-mass craft larger a. Comparison assumes other forces negligible or compares contribution from this interaction only.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: A 2 kg cart pushes a 3 kg cart on a frictionless track. An external 10 N force acts on the 2 kg cart. Find their shared acceleration and contact force; draw both diagrams.
honors.answer: System acceleration 10/5=2 m/s². Contact on 3 kg cart is 6 N; reaction on 2 kg cart is 6 N opposite the applied 10 N.

criteria: Name both objects in an interaction pair.
Place the two equal-and-opposite forces on different objects.
Explain why equal forces can produce unequal accelerations.

title: Free-body diagrams
target: Draw only the external forces on one chosen object.
cpa_model: Choose the object. Draw a dot or box. Add one arrow for each force. Name each source. Motion is not a force. Example: hanging lamp at rest has rope force up and weight down, of equal size.
honors_model: A free-body diagram contains forces on the chosen object, not velocity or additional net-force arrows. Net force is the sum. State which interactions are neglected. Use g=9.8 N/kg.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A fixed-mass cart has acceleration 3 m/s² under 6 N net force. Find acceleration when net force becomes 10 N. Explain.
cpa.answer: Mass 2 kg; new acceleration 5 m/s². At fixed mass, acceleration scales with net force.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw the lamp as a labeled point with its two force arrows. Explain why its force on the cable is not another arrow on this diagram.
cpa.answer: Tension up and weight down; lamp-on-cable force acts on a different object.
cpa.reference:
ΣF_x = ma_x; ΣF_y = ma_y; F_g = mg.
Draw only forces on the chosen object. x and y name directions. Use g = 9.8 N/kg unless another value is given.
cpa.worked: A lamp hangs motionless from one vertical cable. With weight 12 N down, the cable tension is 12 N up. Only forces acting on the lamp belong in its diagram.

cpa.title: A book at rest
cpa.prompt: Draw and label the forces on a book resting on a level table. Name both sources. Use arrows whose comparative lengths match rest.
cpa.answer: Equal normal up and weight down; table and Earth.

visual.caption: The dot represents the object. Object: book

cpa.title: After the hand lets go
cpa.prompt: A box slides to the right on a rough floor after release. Draw its forces. Which way does friction act?
cpa.answer: Weight down, normal up, kinetic friction left; no hand force after release.

cpa.title: A falling ball
cpa.prompt: A ball falls down and is speeding up. Air pushes up. Draw weight and air resistance. Which arrow should be longer?
cpa.answer: Weight down longer than upward drag; net force down.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A cart goes from 18 m to 6 m in 4 s at steady velocity. Find velocity and sketch its position-time graph.
cpa.answer: v=(6-18)/4=-3 m/s, left. Straight descending graph between the stated endpoints.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: A ball moves upward after leaving a hand. Ignore air resistance. Draw its free-body diagram and justify every arrow.
cpa.answer: Only Earth’s weight down. Hand no longer contacts; upward velocity not a force.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Draw separate diagrams for a hanging lamp at rest and the same lamp moving upward at steady speed. What can a force diagram alone fail to tell you?
cpa.answer: Both diagrams can have equal tension and weight. Force balance alone does not tell velocity.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: An a-versus-F_net graph has slope 1.5 (m/s²)/N. Find mass and acceleration at 2.5 N. Explain why a driving-force plot can have an offset.
honors.answer: Mass=1/slope≈0.6667 kg; a=3.75 m/s². Resistance subtracts from driving force, producing an offset.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Draw the lamp as a labeled point with its two force arrows. Explain why its force on the cable is not another arrow on this diagram.
honors.answer: Tension up and weight down; lamp-on-cable force acts on a different object.
honors.reference:
ΣF_x = ma_x; ΣF_y = ma_y; F_g = mg.
Draw only forces on the chosen object. x and y name directions. Use g = 9.8 N/kg unless another value is given.
honors.worked: A lamp hangs motionless from one vertical cable. With weight 12 N down, the cable tension is 12 N up. Only forces acting on the lamp belong in its diagram.

honors.title: Motionless lamp
honors.prompt: A 2 kg lamp hangs from one vertical rope. Draw and label the free-body diagram, including magnitudes.
honors.answer: Tension 19.6 Nup; weight 19.6 N down.

visual.caption: The dot represents the object. Object: 2 kg lamp

honors.title: A rough ramp
honors.prompt: A block rests on a rough incline. Draw weight, normal and static friction. Orient each arrow correctly; explain why weight is not perpendicular to the ramp.
honors.answer: Weight vertically down; normal perpendicular out; static friction up slope opposes gravity’s downslope tendency.

honors.title: Critique the extra arrows
honors.prompt: A diagram of a sliding box includes weight, normal, friction,“velocity force”and“net force.”What must be removed or redrawn? Explain.
honors.answer: Remove velocity force. Show net force separately as a sum, not an additional interaction. Check friction direction and actual sources.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: A straight position-time segment goes from (2 s, -4 m) to (6 s, 20 m). Find velocity, interpret its units and predict x at 8 s if motion continues.
honors.answer: v=6 m/s; position increases 6 m each second. x(8)=32 m.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: A box slides to the left on a rough level floor after release. Draw all forces; state what can be concluded about vertical and horizontal acceleration.
honors.answer: Weight down, normal up, friction right. No vertical acceleration (equal vertical forces); horizontal acceleration right if friction only horizontal force.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: A 4 kg object hangs from two symmetric cables, each 30° from vertical. Use g=10 N/kg. Draw the diagram and calculate each tension.
honors.answer: 2 T cos 30°=40 N, so T≈23.1 N. Horizontal components cancel; do not set each tension to 20 N.

criteria: Choose one object and list its external interactions.
Draw force arrows in physically correct directions.
Remove velocity and net force as extra interaction arrows.

title: From force diagrams to motion
target: Use a force diagram to predict acceleration and velocity change.
cpa_model: Combine forces along each direction, then divide by mass. On a ramp, we will give you gravity’s along-ramp component.CPA problems do not require trigonometry.
honors_model: Choose axes before writing force equations. On a ramp, weight components are mg sinθparallel and mg cosθperpendicular.A component replaces part of the weight description; it is not an extra force.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A 3 kg object has 22 N right and 7 N left. Draw the forces and find net force and acceleration.
cpa.answer: Net force 15 N right; acceleration 5 m/s² right.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw a force diagram and a velocity-time graph that agree. Mark where mass enters the reasoning.
cpa.answer: Net force 4 N right; a=4/2. Straight v-t line from 0 to 6 m/s over 3 s.
cpa.reference:
a_x = ΣF_x/m; a_y = ΣF_y/m.
Choose axes first. CPA ramp problems supply the along-ramp gravity component; no trigonometry is required.
cpa.worked: A 2 kg cart initially at rest has a constant 4 N net force right for 3 s. Acceleration is 2 m/s²; final speed is 6 m/s right.

cpa.title: Horizontal case
cpa.prompt: The diagram shows forces on a 5 kg box. Find net horizontal force and acceleration.
cpa.answer: 30-10=20 N right; a=4 m/s² right.

visual.caption: The dot represents the object. Mass: 5 kg

cpa.title: Use a given ramp component
cpa.prompt: A 2 kg block slides down a ramp. Gravity’s down-ramp component is 10 N; friction is 4 N up the ramp. Find net force and acceleration along the ramp.
cpa.answer: Net 6 N down ramp; a 3 m/s² down ramp.

visual.caption: 10 N down; 4 N up. The marker represents the object on the sloping surface.

cpa.title: Moving up, accelerating down
cpa.prompt: A block slides up a rough ramp after a push ends. Gravity’s along-ramp component and friction both point down the ramp. What happens to its speed?
cpa.answer: Its speed decreases because acceleration opposes up-ramp velocity.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A velocity graph is constant at -5 m/s for 7 s. Find displacement. A second object has components 9 m/s east and 4 m/s south; sketch its direction.
cpa.answer: Displacement -35 m. Second arrow points southeast with component ratio 9: 4.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: A 3 kg cart moves left. It has 15 N right and 6 N left. Find acceleration. Does its leftward speed initially increase or decrease?
cpa.answer: Net 9 N right; a 3 m/s² right; leftward speed decreases.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: A 3 kg cart has 5 N right and 26 N left. Find acceleration. What else must you know to decide if it speeds up?
honors.answer: Net -21 N; a=-7 m/s². Need current velocity: leftward motion speeds up; rightward motion slows.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Draw a force diagram and a velocity-time graph that agree. Mark where mass enters the reasoning.
honors.answer: Net force 4 N right; a=4/2. Straight v-t line from 0 to 6 m/s over 3 s.
honors.reference:
Fg, parallel = mg sin θ; Fg, perpendicular = mg cos θ; ΣF = ma.
Ramp angle θ above horizontal. Components replace the weight vector; they are not extra forces.
honors.worked: A 2 kg cart initially at rest has a constant 4 N net force right for 3 s. Acceleration is 2 m/s²; final speed is 6 m/s right.

honors.title: Angled pull
honors.prompt: A 5 kg box stays on a level floor.A rope pulls with components 20 N right and 12 Nup; friction is 5 N left. Find normal force and horizontal acceleration. Use g=9.8.
honors.answer: N=49-12=37 N; net x 15 N; a_x 3 m/s² right.

visual.caption: The dot represents the object. Normal not shown; find it

honors.title: Frictionless ramp
honors.prompt: A 2 kg cart slides down a 20° frictionless ramp. Find normal force and acceleration along the ramp. Use g=9.8 m/s².
honors.answer: N=mg cos 20=18.4 N; a=g sin 20=3.35 m/s² down.

visual.caption: The marker represents the object on the sloping surface.

honors.title: Oppose upward motion

honors.answer: a=(-4×9.8×.5-5)/4=-6.15 m/s²; slowing while moving up.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: Velocity is +5 m/s for 7 s, then -4 m/s for 5 s. Find displacement and distance. Explain the reference information needed for an angle of 35°.
honors.answer: Displacement 15 m; distance 55 m. An angle needs a reference direction/axis and rotation sense.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: A 2 kg block slides down a 30° ramp with 3.8 N friction up the ramp. Find along-ramp acceleration and normal force. Use g=9.8.
honors.answer: Weight parallel 9.8 N; net 6 N down; a 3 m/s² down; N=16.97≈17.0 N.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: A 2 kg cart moving right at 8 m/s has a constant 4 N net force left for 6 s. Find when it turns, final velocity, displacement and distance.
honors.answer: a=-2; turns at 4 s; v_f=-4 m/s; displacement 48-36=12 m; distance 16+4=20 m.

criteria: Write a force sum along each chosen axis.

title: Static and kinetic friction
target: Distinguish adjustable static friction from sliding friction.
cpa_model: Static friction adjusts to prevent slipping, up to a limit. If you push 5 N and the box stays still, friction is 5 N opposite. Kinetic friction acts while the surfaces slide.
honors_model: 0≤f_s≤μ_sN; maximum static friction=μ_sN. Kinetic friction magnitude=μ_k N when sliding. Check for vertical acceleration or other vertical forces before assuming N=mg.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A runner pushes the ground backward with 50 N. Name the partner force, its size and the object it acts on. Explain its role in the runner’s motion.
cpa.answer: Ground pushes the runner’s foot forward with 50 N. This external force can accelerate the runner; the partner forces act on different objects.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw the horizontal forces. Then redraw for a 5 N push that is still below the maximum.
cpa.answer: Balanced 3 N pair, then balanced 5 N pair. Friction adjusts while the box remains at rest.
cpa.reference:
0 ≤ f_s ≤ μ_s N; f_k = μ_k N.
s = static; k = kinetic; N = normal force. Static friction adjusts up to its maximum. Kinetic friction applies during sliding.
cpa.worked: A box remains still while pushed with 3 N. Static friction is 3 N opposite the push, provided its maximum is at least 3 N. Static friction need not equal its maximum.

cpa.title: Below the limit
cpa.prompt: The box stays at rest with an 8 N push right. Maximum static friction is 15 N. Find actual friction and net force.
cpa.answer: Actual 8 N left; net 0 N, not 15 N friction.

visual.caption: The dot represents the object. At rest; static limit 15 N

cpa.title: Crossing the limit
cpa.prompt: For the same box, the push increases to 18 N. Sliding friction is 12 N. Once it slides right, find net force.
cpa.answer: 18>15 N starts slipping; net 18-12=6 N right.

cpa.title: Can friction help?
cpa.prompt: Your foot pushes backward on the ground without slipping. Which way does ground friction act on your foot? Explain why“friction always points backward”is wrong.
cpa.answer: Forward. It opposes relative slipping or tendency at the contact, not always the person’s motion.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A cart starts at 4 m and moves right at 6 m/s for 3 s. Predict final position. Allowed endpoints are 20 to 24 m; state this interval and one assumption.
cpa.answer: Central position 22 m; interval 20-24 m. Assumes steady velocity and the stated start.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: Maximum static friction is 20 N.A 12 N push does not move the box. Find actual friction.A 25 N push starts sliding with 16 N kinetic friction: find net force.
cpa.answer: First 12 N opposite push; second 9 N in the direction of the push.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: A box has maximum static friction 8 N and kinetic friction 6 N. Predict the behavior for pushes of 4, 8 and 10 N. Draw the sliding case.
cpa.answer: 4 N: rest possible with 4 N friction. 8 N: limiting equilibrium. 10 N: starts sliding; net 4 N in push direction once moving.
