honors.answer: Equal opposite 15 N forces. Craft acceleration 5 m/s²; asteroid 0.05 m/s² opposite. Compares this interaction’s contribution, or assumes other forces negligible.

honors.title: Explain a worked example

honors.answer: Balanced 3 N pair, then balanced 5 N pair. Friction adjusts while the box remains at rest.
honors.reference:
0 ≤ f_s ≤ μ_s N; f_k = μ_k N.
s = static; k = kinetic; N = normal force. Static friction adjusts up to its maximum. Kinetic friction applies during sliding.
honors.worked: A box remains still while pushed with 3 N. Static friction is 3 N opposite the push, provided its maximum is at least 3 N. Static friction need not equal its maximum.

honors.answer: Means 8 N and 6 N;μ_s≈.40 andμ_k≈.30; static coefficient gives limiting threshold.

honors.answer: Central 44 m; half-width 1.3 m; interval [42.7, 45.3] m; full width 2.6 m. Constant velocity and bounded input ranges.

honors.answer: N 98 N; static limit 49 N.30 N case: friction 30 N, a 0.60 N case: friction 39.2 N, a 2.08 m/s².

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: A 5 kg box has μ_s=0.4 and μ_k=0.3 on a level floor; use g=10 N/kg. A horizontal 22 N pull begins from rest. Find maximum static friction, acceleration after motion starts, and the pull needed for steady sliding.
honors.answer: N=50 N, f_s, max=20 N; 22 exceeds it. Kinetic friction 15 N, acceleration 7/5=1.4 m/s². Steady sliding requires 15 N.

title: Equilibrium and missing forces
target: Find a missing force when acceleration is zero.
cpa_model: Equilibrium means balanced forces and zero acceleration. It can mean rest or straight motion at steady speed. Example: 10 N right needs 10 N left to balance.
honors_model: Equilibrium requiresΣF_x=0 andΣF_y=0. In two-rope symmetry, horizontal components cancel and vertical components must support weight. Use g=9.8 N/kg.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A 3 kg ball is moving upward at 5 m/s after leaving a hand. Ignore air resistance; use g=10 N/kg. Draw and justify its free-body diagram.
cpa.answer: Only weight 30 N downward from Earth. The hand is no longer in contact; upward velocity is not a force.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw and label all three forces. Identify the equation that checks vertical balance.
cpa.answer: 4+6-10=0 N; upward total equals downward total.
cpa.reference:
ΣF_x = 0; ΣF_y = 0 ⇒ a = 0.
Equilibrium allows rest or constant velocity. Resolve missing forces along each axis. Use g = 9.8 N/kg.

title: Gravity above the surface

cpa_model: At altitude h above a spherical planet of radius R, r=R+h. Field ratio g_h/g_surface=[R/(R+h)]².

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw the radius and altitude as different line segments. Mark the full center-to-object distance.
cpa.answer: Radius R plus altitude 2 R makes 3 R; using h alone gives the wrong denominator.
cpa.reference:
r = R + h; g_h/g_surface = [R/(R + h)]².
R is planet radius; h is altitude. g_h is field strength at altitude h.
cpa.worked: At altitude h=2 R above a planet's surface, center distance is r=R+h=3 R. A surface field of 18 N/kg becomes 18/9=2 N/kg.

title: Independent projectile directions
target: Explain why horizontal and vertical projectile motion share time but evolve differently.

honors_model: In ideal near-Earth projectile motion, a_x=0 and a_y is downward. Horizontal velocity stays constant. Use g=10 m/s² for today’s numbers.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A 3 kg test mass feels 15 N toward a source. Find g and the force on a 7 kg mass at the same point.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example

criteria: Use center-to-center distance.
Explain why negative potential energy does not mean negative kinetic energy.
Compute changes from final minus initial energy.
cpa_model: Outside a spherical source, U=-GMm/r when U=0 at infinity. Moving outward makes U less negative. ΔU=U_final-U_initial.
honors_model: Outside a spherical source, U=-GMm/r when U=0 at infinity. Moving outward makes U less negative. ΔU=U_final-U_initial.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A cart’s work is measured over the first 3 m, but its speed change is measured over 5 m. Can these values directly test W_net=ΔK? Explain.
cpa.answer: No. Work and kinetic-energy change must refer to the same endpoints. Measure matching intervals.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw an energy number line and mark the direction toward the zero at infinite separation.
cpa.answer: -40 to -20 moves toward zero; outward motion increases U.
cpa.reference:
U = -GMm/r; ΔU = U_f - U_i.
Outside a spherical source; choose U = 0 at infinity. Moving outward makes U less negative.
cpa.worked: For a supplied source with GMm=120 J·m, potential energy is U=-120/r. At r=3 m, U=-40 J; at 6 m, U=-20 J. Moving outward raises U by 20 J.

cpa.title: Look and explain
cpa.prompt: An object moves outward from r to 2 r. Does gravitational potential energy become more or less negative? Draw a number-line comparison.
cpa.answer: Less negative: U magnitude halves.

cpa.title: Build the solution

cpa.title: Use the idea
cpa.prompt: A student says “negative potential energy means the object has negative kinetic energy.” Correct the claim.
cpa.answer: Potential zero is convention; kinetic energy½mv² is non negative. Total can be negative for bound motion.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: In the same straight-line deflection model, keep sideways Δv fixed but make lead time 4 times as long. Compare shift and name a limitation.
cpa.answer: Shift becomes 4 times as large: shift=Δv×time. The toy model omits orbital curvature/gravity and uncertainties.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: U changes from-10 J to-6 J. CalculateΔU and state whether the object gained gravitational energy.
cpa.answer: +4 J; gained.

cpa.answer: -30 and -10 J; outward change +20 J.

cpa_model: Sliding without rotation can use K=½mv². Rolling objects also have rotational kinetic energy. An ideal pendulum exchanges gravitational and kinetic energy while constraints guide the path.

K_translation = ½mv²; K_total = K_translation + K_rotation.
A rolling object also rotates. Track all energy forms; an ideal pendulum exchanges gravitational and kinetic energy.

title: Heat is not temperature
target: Distinguish temperature from energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
criteria: Compare temperature with thermal energy.
Identify the direction of spontaneous heat transfer.
Explain why amount and material matter.
cpa_model: Temperature describes thermal state. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. A larger sample at the same temperature can store more internal energy.
honors_model: Temperature describes thermal state. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. A larger sample at the same temperature can store more internal energy.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A toy model requires 15 J to escape, but an object has only 12 J and no later energy input. Does the model predict escape? Explain.
cpa.answer: No; it lacks 3 J of the required energy and remains bound under the model.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw equal temperature indicators but different amounts of water. Predict heat-flow direction if the water samples are brought into thermal contact at the same temperature.
cpa.answer: Same-temperature samples have no net heat flow due to a temperature difference; larger amount generally stores more internal energy for the same material/state.
cpa.reference:
Q = mcΔT.
For heating without a phase change: Q is transferred heat, m is mass, c is specific heat. Heat and temperature are different quantities.
cpa.worked: A cup and a bathtub can both be at 40°C. Equal temperature does not imply equal internal energy: amount and type of material also matter.

cpa.title: Look and explain
cpa.prompt: A cup and a bathtub contain the same substance at 40°C. Are their temperatures equal? Must their total internal energies be equal?

title: Conduction, convection, radiation
target: Identify mechanisms of heat transfer and support each classification.
criteria: Describe contact transfer, bulk fluid motion and electromagnetic transfer.

cpa_model: Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions in matter. Convection involves bulk fluid motion. Thermal radiation travels by electromagnetic waves and can cross a vacuum.
honors_model: Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions in matter. Convection involves bulk fluid motion. Thermal radiation travels by electromagnetic waves and can cross a vacuum.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea

E_i + E_in = E_f + E_out.
Account for energy across the system boundary. Conduction: matter interactions; convection: fluid motion; radiation: electromagnetic waves.
cpa.worked: A metal rod transfers energy from its hot end toward its cool end by conduction. A circulating fluid can carry energy by convection; radiation can cross a vacuum.

title: Phase changes

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea

Q = mL; Q = mcΔT.
Use mL during a phase change at constant temperature, and mcΔT outside that interval. L is latent heat.
cpa.worked: Melting 2 kg of a substance with latent heat 100 J/kg requires 200 J. During ideal melting at fixed pressure, added energy changes phase without raising temperature.

title: Temperature and particle motion
target: Use a particle model to distinguish average motion from total energy.
criteria: Describe temperature in terms of microscopic motion.

cpa_model: For an ideal gas, average translational kinetic energy per particle is proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin. A gas contains a range of particle speeds.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw two equal-size samples using dots and arrows; label arrows as particle velocities and make the warmer sample's average arrow length greater.
cpa.answer: Warmer sample has greater average motion, not necessarily every particle faster than every colder one.
cpa.reference:
K_avg ∝ T; T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
Ideal gas: mean translational kinetic energy per particle scales with absolute temperature. ∝ means proportional to.
cpa.worked: In a gas model, warmer temperature corresponds to greater average random molecular kinetic energy. Individual particles still have a range of speeds.

cpa.title: Look and explain

title: Refraction
target: Connect a change in wave speed to wavelength and direction.
criteria: Measure ray angles from the normal.

cpa_model: At a stationary boundary, frequency stays the same while speed and wavelength can change. A ray entering a slower medium bends toward the normal, except at normal incidence.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw and label the boundary, normal, incident ray and refracted ray.
cpa.answer: Refracted angle to normal smaller in the slower medium, for ordinary positive-index media.

v₁ = fλ₁; v₂ = fλ₂; λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁.

title: Diffraction

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea

λ = v/f; compare opening width with λ.

title: Intensity, decibels and Doppler
target: Distinguish intensity change from frequency shift.
criteria: Use an intensity ratio separately from pitch.
Interpret a logarithmic sound-level difference.
Predict approach and recession Doppler trends.
cpa_model: Sound level difference Δβ=10 log₁₀(I₂/I₁). A tenfold intensity increase gives 10 dB. For approach, observed sound frequency is typically higher; recession gives lower frequency.
honors_model: Sound level difference Δβ=10 log₁₀(I₂/I₁). A tenfold intensity increase gives 10 dB. For approach, observed sound frequency is typically higher; recession gives lower frequency.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A 500 Hz sound travels through air. Do air particles mainly move parallel or perpendicular to propagation? Name the wave type.
cpa.answer: Parallel oscillation; a longitudinal pressure wave.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw two concentric wavefronts and indicate why the outer surface shares the power more widely.
cpa.answer: Area proportional to r²; total power conserved while intensity decreases.
cpa.reference:
Δβ = 10 log₁₀(I₂/I₁).
I is intensity; β is sound level in dB. Tenfold intensity gives +10 dB. Approach generally raises observed frequency; recession lowers it.
cpa.worked: For the same point source, doubling distance spreads its power over four times the area, so ideal intensity drops to one quarter. This assumes spherical spreading without extra absorption.

cpa.title: Look and explain
cpa.prompt: A moving source approaches a stationary listener, then recedes. Sketch closer wavefront spacing in front and wider spacing behind; compare heard pitch.
cpa.answer: Higher on approach, lower on recession in basic Doppler model.

title: Thermal radiation and color
target: Use peak wavelength as one piece of evidence about a thermal spectrum.
criteria: Relate higher temperature to shorter peak wavelength.
Use kelvin in Wien’s law.
Distinguish spectral peak from perceived color.
cpa_model: For an ideal blackbody,λ_max T=2.9×10⁻³ m·K. Hotter means a shorter peak wavelength. Perceived color combines the visible spectrum; real meteor spectra can also contain emission lines.
honors_model: For an ideal blackbody,λ_max T=2.9×10⁻³ m·K. Hotter means a shorter peak wavelength. Perceived color combines the visible spectrum; real meteor spectra can also contain emission lines.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A light ray strikes a plane mirror at 20° from the normal. Find the reflection angle and label both angles on a sketch.
cpa.answer: 20° from the normal, on the other side.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Sketch two broad thermal spectra, labeling axes and the hotter peak's shift.
cpa.answer: Hotter curve peaks at shorter wavelength; visible color cannot be inferred from one peak alone without the full spectrum/observer context.
cpa.reference:
λ_max T = 2.9×10⁻³ m·K.
Ideal blackbody; T in kelvin, λ_max in meters. A shorter peak wavelength means higher temperature, not one exact visible color.
cpa.worked: A thermal spectrum's peak shifts toward shorter wavelength as absolute temperature rises. Wien's relationλ_peak T≈2.9×10⁻³ m·K givesλ_peak≈9.7 micrometers at 300 K.

cpa.title: Look and explain
cpa.prompt: Two ideal thermal emitters are at 3000 and 6000 K. Which has the shorter peak wavelength? Does that mean they emit only one color?
cpa.answer: 6000 K; no, broad spectra.

cpa.title: Build the solution
cpa.prompt: Supplied peaks: 3000 K gives about 970 nm; 6000 K gives about 480 nm. Compare wavelengths and identify which peak is outside visible light (roughly 400-700 nm).
cpa.answer: Hotter peak about half; 970 nm infrared outside visible.

cpa.title: Use the idea
cpa.prompt: An object has an infrared peak but looks red-hot. Explain how both can be true.
cpa.answer: Broad thermal spectrum still has visible redtail; peak need not be in visible band.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: An upward rope pulse is 4 cm high before reaching an ideal free end. Is the reflected displacement upright or inverted? Sketch it.
cpa.answer: Upright. An ideal free-end reflection does not invert the displacement pulse.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: Absolute temperature doubles. How does peak wavelength change?
cpa.answer: Halves.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: If temperature doubles, compare peak wavelengths. Explain why a room-temperature object can radiate even when it is not visibly glowing.
cpa.answer: Peak wavelength halves; much radiation is infrared.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: An object moves 0.3 m toward a fixed plane mirror. Find image movement and the change in object-image separation.
honors.answer: Image moves 0.3 m toward the mirror from behind it. Separation decreases by 0.6 m.

honors.title: Explain a worked example

honors.title: Represent and interpret
honors.prompt: Two ideal thermal emitters are at 3000 and 6000 K. Which has the shorter peak wavelength? Does that mean they emit only one color?
honors.answer: 6000 K; no, broad spectra.

honors.title: Solve and justify
honors.prompt: Calculateλ_max for 5000 K and 10, 000 K. Convert to nm. Explain why you should not assign an exact observed meteor color from the peak alone.
honors.answer: 580 nm; 290 nm(UV). Observed color uses whole spectrum and may include emission lines/atmospheric effects.

honors.title: Analyze the reasoning
honors.prompt: An object has an infrared peak but looks red-hot. Explain how both can be true.
honors.answer: Broad thermal spectrum still has visible redtail; peak need not be in visible band.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: Across a stationary boundary, frequency remains 4 Hz while speed changes from 24 to 32 m/s. Find both wavelengths.
honors.answer: First λ=6 m; second λ=8 m, using λ=v/f.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: An ideal blackbody hasλ_max=725 nm. Estimate temperature.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: Find peak wavelengths at 3000 and 6000 K. State why wavelength peak alone does not specify one exact perceived color.
honors.answer: ≈967 and 483 nm; broad emission, visual sensitivity and conditions determine appearance, not one spectral wavelength.

title: Mechanical waves and distant effects

criteria: Identify the medium carrying the wave.

honors_model: Seismic and water waves transfer disturbances through matter. Speeds depend on the wave type and medium. Use only supplied classroom values; these are not real hazard forecasts.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A bundle of parallel rays passes through a lens and becomes 3 times as wide farther beyond it, with rays spreading immediately after the lens. Identify the lens type and sketch the rays.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw the two waves and two corresponding relative-intensity bars.
cpa.answer: Half amplitude; quarter intensity under the stated same-medium model.
cpa.reference:
d = vΔt; Δt = d/v.
Use the supplied wave speed for its medium and wave type. These classroom models are not real hazard forecasts.
cpa.worked: In a simple model, a wave amplitude falls from 4 to 2 units while intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. Intensity becomes one quarter, not one half.

title: Transfer: waves and signals

criteria: Use wave speed and round-trip geometry correctly.

State the limits of an inference from a signal.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: A radar echo’s complete outward-and-return path is 5000 m. Find the target range and explain the division.
cpa.answer: 2500 m; range is half the full path.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw a measurement plan labeling outgoing pulse, return pulse and the time interval.
cpa.answer: Round-trip timing plus propagation speed gives range; a separate frequency comparison helps determine radial motion.
cpa.reference:
v = fλ; T = 1/f; d_range = vΔt/2.
d_range is one-way range from round-trip time. Match speed and model to the wave and medium.
cpa.worked: An echo time measures range using travel speed, while a frequency shift can indicate radial motion. Different observations answer different questions about the same target.

cpa.title: Look and explain
cpa.prompt: Sketch a wave and label amplitude and wavelength. Explain which tells about oscillation size and which about spatial repetition.
cpa.answer: Amplitude: size from equilibrium; wavelength: distance between matching phase points.

cpa.title: Build the solution
cpa.prompt: A wave has f=5 Hz andλ=2 m. Find v.A toy echo at that speed returns after 4 s; find range.

cpa.answer: The 6 cm wave generally spreads more because wavelength is larger relative to the same opening.

cpa.title: Exit check

honors.answer: At the same wave speed, equal range gives equal out-and-back time. Doppler shift depends on radial velocity, so motion can differ.

honors.answer: Thermal peak halves by Wien; soundλhalves at fixed sound speed.

title: Charge and the electric car
target: Explain charge interactions and trace an electric car’s energy transfers.
criteria: Predict attraction or repulsion from charge signs.
Distinguish charge from energy.
Trace energy from a battery to moving wheels.
cpa_model: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. A battery transfers energy to a circuit; charge already exists in its wires. A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy and thermal energy.
honors_model: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. A battery transfers energy to a circuit; charge already exists in its wires. A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy and thermal energy.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: An ideal blackbody’s kelvin temperature becomes 3 times as large. How does its peak wavelength change?
cpa.answer: It becomes 1/3 as large by Wien’s law.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw before-and-after charge accounts for both objects. Distinguish transfer from creation of charge.
cpa.answer: Opposite changes-3 and+3; total charge conserved for the isolated pair.
cpa.reference:
E_electrical = E_mechanical + E_thermal + other transfers.
Energy accounting for a motor with no net energy storage. A battery transfers energy; charge already exists in the wires.
cpa.worked: Rubbing can transfer electrons between materials. If one isolated object gains charge-3 units and another loses the same electrons, their charge changes add to zero.

cpa.title: Look and explain
cpa.prompt: Draw force arrows for two positive charges, then for a positive and a negative charge.
cpa.answer: Like signs repel; opposite signs attract. Forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

visual.caption: Each circle represents one of the labeled objects or charges; r is their center-to-center separation.

cpa.title: Build the solution
cpa.prompt: Put these energy forms in order: car motion, chemical energy in battery, electrical transfer, motor rotation. Name one less useful transfer.

cpa.title: Use the idea
cpa.prompt: A student says the motor uses up the current so less returns to the battery. Explain the mistake for a steady series circuit.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: Two wave displacements at one point are -4 mm and +8 mm. Find the resultant and state whether they reinforce or partly cancel.
cpa.answer: +4 mm; partly cancel.

cpa.title: Exit check

cpa.answer: Repulsion.

cpa.answer: No; a charged object can attract a neutral polarizable object. Like net charges repel in the simple model.

r is separation. Signs determine attraction/repulsion; the equation gives magnitude.

title: Magnetic fields

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea

title: Electromagnetic induction

cpa.title: Use the idea
cpa.prompt: One run stops early after a loose connection. Should you erase it? Explain how to record it fairly and decide whether it belongs in a speed comparison.
cpa.answer: Retain and annotate failure; report completed-run speeds separately with inclusion criteria and failure count.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A magnet moves through a 60-turn coil. Propose two controlled changes that could increase induced-emf magnitude and explain each.
cpa.answer: Faster flux change or more turns increases emf magnitude. Stronger field/effective area changes are valid with suitable controls.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: Name the final design change you will keep and cite one specific observation or measurement supporting it.
cpa.answer: Student cites actual evidence and acknowledges if evidence is limited.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Return to the worked example in problem 2. Compare this set with 2.1, 2.1, 2.1 s. Discuss speed and consistency rather than declaring one winner from the fastest run alone.
cpa.answer: Second set faster mean 2.1 s and more consistent; first has fastest individual run 2.0 s. Choice depends on stated criteria.

honors.title: Bring back an earlier idea
honors.prompt: A 50-tooth driver turns a 350-tooth gear. Give ideal output/input torque and speed ratios and state the loss assumption.
honors.answer: Torque ratio 7; speed ratio 1/7. Assumes ideal gears with negligible losses.

honors.title: Explain a worked example
honors.prompt: Make a trial table and mark both mean and fastest time.
honors.answer: All three retained; mean≈2.17 s, fastest 2.0 s.
honors.reference:
mean time = sum of trial times/number of trials; average speed = distance/time.
Measure course length; keep release and timing consistent. Retain every trial and required build evidence.
honors.worked: Supplied 3 m runs take 2.0, 2.4, 2.1 s. Report all trials; their mean time is 2.17 s. “Fastest run 2.0 s” answers a different question from typical performance.

honors.title: Represent and interpret
honors.prompt: Complete a final labeled sketch or attach a photo with labels. Identify a feature that supports straight motion and one that supports reliable electrical operation.
honors.answer: Actual evidence with functional labels and explanations.

honors.title: Solve and justify
honors.prompt: Supplied times over 4.0 m are 5.0, 5.2 and 4.8 s. Find mean time, time range and speed calculated from mean time.
honors.answer: Mean 5.0 s; range .4 s; .80 m/s from mean time.

honors.title: Analyze the reasoning
honors.prompt: One run stops early after a loose connection. Should you erase it? Explain how to record it fairly and decide whether it belongs in a speed comparison.
honors.answer: Retain and annotate failure; report completed-run speeds separately with inclusion criteria and failure count.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: The same flux change through the same coil occurs in 1/4 of the time. Compare induced-emf magnitude and name a condition for that comparison.
honors.answer: Emf is 4 times as large. Same turn count and flux change per turn; compare average emf over each interval.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: Write a three-sentence claim-evidence-reasoning explanation for a design choice. Distinguish a controlled comparison from a plausible mechanism only.
honors.answer: Claim is bounded; numerical/observational evidence named; physical mechanism fits; causal certainty matches the comparison.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: For 3 m runs of 2.0 and 3.0 s, compare mean of the two speeds with total distance divided by total time. Explain why the results differ.
honors.answer: Mean speeds (1.5+1.0)/2=1.25 m/s; total 6/5=1.2 m/s. Equal-trial and time-weighted averaging differ.

title: Race, explain and transfer
target: Evaluate a model against measured performance and defend design decisions.
criteria: Report measured distance, time and average speed.
Compare actual speed with a stated prediction.
Use evidence to explain three physical design choices.
cpa_model: Record the actual race conditions and result. Relative deviation from prediction=|measured-predicted|/|predicted|×100%, when predicted is nonzero. This is a comparison with a prediction, not the symmetric percent-difference formula.
honors_model: Record the actual race conditions and result. Relative deviation from prediction=|measured-predicted|/|predicted|×100%, when predicted is nonzero. This is a comparison with a prediction, not the symmetric percent-difference formula.
note: Keep the official race/judging record separate from these supplied practice examples. Report your own results honestly.

cpa.title: Bring back an earlier idea
cpa.prompt: At unchanged wheel rpm, circumference becomes 6 times as large. Compare ideal travel speed and state one real-world limitation.
cpa.answer: Ideal speed becomes 6 times as large. Actual rpm, load or slipping may change.

cpa.title: Explain a worked example
cpa.prompt: Draw an energy-flow diagram from battery to motion and other transfers; annotate it with one actual result, clearly labeled as measured.
cpa.answer: Electrical input to motor/mechanical motion plus thermal/sound transfers; actual measurements distinguished from illustrative values.
cpa.reference:
average speed = distance/time; relative deviation = |measured - predicted|/|predicted| × 100%.
Prediction must be nonzero. Record real race conditions; this compares with a prediction, not symmetric percent difference.
cpa.worked: A car covers 3 m in 2 s: average speed 1.5 m/s. A complete explanation also uses its circuit, gearing, friction and evidence from repeated runs; one race time does not isolate a cause.

cpa.title: Look and explain
cpa.prompt: Draw or annotate your final car. Label three choices involving wheels, gears, alignment, wiring or mass, then connect each to a physics idea.
cpa.answer: Three supported explanations using relevant mechanics/circuit ideas.

cpa.title: Build the solution
cpa.prompt: A supplied car travels 5 m in 10 s. Find measured speed. Its prediction was .60 m/s. Use the supplied difference .10 m/s to calculate relative deviation=.10÷.60×100%.
cpa.answer: .50 m/s; 16.7% below the prediction.

cpa.title: Use the idea
cpa.prompt: Use your actual race record to defend one successful design choice and identify one revision for a future build. Cite data or a specific observation for each.
cpa.answer: Actual evidence and bounded explanations; a lower race placing alone does not diagnose a cause.

cpa.title: Choose a method
cpa.prompt: A device receives 60 J mechanical energy at its shaft and produces electrical energy at its terminals. Identify it and name one possible loss.
cpa.answer: A generator. Some energy can become heating, friction or sound.

cpa.title: Exit check
cpa.prompt: Choose one problem on this sheet. Circle your current 1, 2 or 3 self-check and name the next step that would improve your explanation.
cpa.answer: Student names a concrete next step tied to evidence or a skill; self-rating is not a teacher score.

cpa.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
cpa.prompt: Propose one redesign and predict two possible effects, including a tradeoff. State the measurement that would support or challenge your prediction.
cpa.answer: Example lower gearing may improve starting torque but reduce unloaded speed; test start reliability and timed speed under controlled conditions.

honors.title: Solve and justify
honors.prompt: A supplied car travels 6.0 m in 8.0 s; predicted speed is .90 m/s. Calculate measured speed, relative deviation and a plausible source of mismatch.
honors.answer: .75 m/s; 16.7% below prediction; load, slip, friction or model assumptions, with evidence needed to attribute cause.

honors.title: Analyze the reasoning
honors.prompt: Use your actual race record to defend one successful design choice and identify one revision for a future build. Cite data or a specific observation for each.
honors.answer: Actual evidence and bounded explanations; a lower race placing alone does not diagnose a cause.

honors.title: Choose a method
honors.prompt: A motor is 64% efficient and the following generator is 72% efficient. Find the combined useful fraction in sequence.
honors.answer: Combined fraction=0.4608 or 46.08%, multiplying the two efficiencies.

honors.title: Exit check
honors.prompt: Transfer: a similar car uses twice the wheel diameter with the same loaded wheel rpm. Predict ideal speed change, then explain why testing is still necessary.
honors.answer: Ideal speed doubles; increased required torque, loading, slip and clearance may change actual rpm/performance.

honors.title: STRETCH: Apply it another way
honors.prompt: Supplied input is 6 V×1 A for 4 s. A 0.5 kg car reaches 2 m/s on a level track from rest. Find input energy and final translational kinetic energy. Explain why their ratio alone is not total drivetrain efficiency.
honors.answer: Input 24 J; K 1 J; ratio≈4.17%. Also account for rotational energy, work against resistance, stored energy and time history.
